unit.can_do_en: talk with the daycare and school about my children.

brief.situation_en: Maria calls the daycare in the morning.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Hi, this is Maria, Lucas's mum.

judge.reason: Moi and Hei are both greetings; the rest is identical.
Moi and Hei are register variants of the same greeting.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Lucas on kipee tänään. Se ei tuu päiväkotiin.
lines.text_kirja: Lucas on sairas tänään. Hän ei tule päiväkotiin.
lines.gloss_en: Lucas is ill today. He won't come to daycare.

judge.reason: Kipee and sairas both mean sick; se and hän both refer to Lucas; tuu is the spoken form of tule.

puhe.text: Lucas on kipee tänään. Se ei tuu päiväkotiin.

kirja.text: Lucas on sairas tänään. Hän ei tule päiväkotiin.

lines.speaker: Sari
lines.gloss_en: Oh no. Does he have a fever?

judge.reason: Onks sil is the spoken form of onko hänellä; both ask whether he has a fever.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Yes, a little. And a runny nose.

judge.reason: Joo and kyllä both mean yes; the content is the same.

lines.speaker: Sari
lines.gloss_en: OK, thanks for letting us know. Get well soon!

judge.reason: Kiitti and kiitos both mean thanks; pikasta and pikaista both mean quick; same wish.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Kiitti. Mä ilmotan, kun se on terve.
lines.text_kirja: Kiitos. Minä ilmoitan, kun hän on terve.
lines.gloss_en: Thanks. I'll let you know when he's well.

judge.reason: Same meaning: I will let you know when he is well; only the register differs.

puhe.text: Kiitti. Mä ilmotan, kun se on terve.

kirja.text: Kiitos. Minä ilmoitan, kun hän on terve.

judge.reason: Moikka and Näkemiin are both farewells that differ only in register.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

The form of olla, to be, for he, she or it. People say it the same way.
Speech often says kipee for ill. Books write sairas.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech uses se for a person. Books write hän.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. People say it the same way.
After ei the verb drops its ending: tulla becomes tule. Speech shortens it to tuu.
Adds -iin for 'to': päiväkoti becomes päiväkotiin.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: On with -ko to ask a question. Speech often says -ks: onks.
Hän takes -llä for 'has': hänellä on. Speech uses se and says sil.
The partitive singular is used for an illness you have: kuume becomes kuumetta.
Joo is the everyday spoken yes. Books write kyllä.

Kiitti is the everyday spoken thanks. Books write kiitos.
Kiitos takes -sta for the thing you thank for: tieto becomes tiedosta, with t changing to d.
The partitive singular, used in wishes: pikainen becomes pikaista. Speech drops the i: pikasta.
A noun made from the verb parata 'to get better', in the partitive used for wishes: paranemista.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Ilmoittaa changes to ilmoita- and takes -n for 'I': ilmoitan. Speech drops an i: ilmotan.
